[9] The Court has, in many cases, considered the IRCC service standards or processing timelines to determine whether there has been an unreasonable delay. See for instance: Kia v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2026 FC 780 [Kia].

[10] As the Court explained in Kia at para 15: “While not determinative, service standards for study permit applications are relevant to the inquiry of how much time is required by the nature of the process”.

[11] However, the problem in this case is that the Applicant has not adduced any evidence about the IRCC service standards for study permit applications. As IRCC processing timelines vary over time, I cannot determine, in an evidentiary vacuum, which service standard applies in the Applicant’s case. For instance, I note that in Kia, the service standard was 60 days at the time the applicant submitted their study permit application and that “increased to 41 weeks as of February 2025 under the dynamic processing time”, Kia at para 15.

[12] As the Applicant bears the onus of demonstrating that he meets the test for mandamus, I find that the Applicant’s failure to adduce relevant evidence about the service standard undermines his argument about the unreasonableness of the delay.

[13] But even assuming that there has been an unreasonable delay, I find that the Respondent has provided a reasonable justification for the delay.

[14] According to the Global Case Management System notes, on April 30, 2025, the IRCC requested the Applicant to submit his military records. The Applicant responded to the IRCC’s inquiry on May 14, 2025. The Respondent has also provided evidence that no decision has been made due to the pending security screening. The Respondent relies on IRCC’s website to argue that complex or non-routine applications may take “longer than the normal processing time to review” and that given the Applicant’s SP application is undergoing background checks, it can result in longer processing times.

[15] While he was given the opportunity to do so, the Applicant did not make any submission in reply. As such, the Applicant’s only submission before the Court is that the Respondent failed to provide any explanation for the delay.

REASONS AND JUDGMENT

I. Overview [1] Seyyed Hossein Samiei [Applicant], a citizen of Iran, is seeking a writ of mandamus compelling Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada [IRCC] to decide his application for a study permit [SP application].

[2] The parties jointly request that this application for judicial review be determined in writing, pursuant to paragraph 68 of the Consolidated Practice Guidelines for Citizenship, Immigration, and Refugee Protection Proceedings (August 12, 2026).

[3] I dismiss the application. The Applicant fails to adduce evidence to demonstrate that there has been unreasonable delay, and the Respondent has provided a reasonable justification for the delay. The balance of convenience does not favour granting a mandamus order.

II. Analysis [4] The Applicant must demonstrate to the Court’s satisfaction that he meets the mandamus test as set out in Apotex Inc v Canada (Attorney General)(CA), 1993 CanLII 3004 (FCTAD), [1994] 1 FC 742 (FCA) at 766-69.

[6] The Court outlined three requirements that must be met if a delay is to be considered unreasonable in Conille v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration) (TD), 1998 CanLII 9097 (FC) at para 23:
1.The delay in question has been longer than the nature of the process required, prima facie;
2.The applicant and his counsel are not responsible for the delay; and
3.The authority responsible for the delay has not provided satisfactory justification.

[7] Based on the parties’ submissions, the contentious issues in this case focus on whether the Respondent has refused to perform their duty, whether the delay was unreasonable, whether the Respondent has provided a justification for the delay, and whether the balance of convenience favours the issuance of a mandamus order.

[8] The Applicant submits that the delay of 15 months after submitting the SP application is unreasonable, when according to the IRCC’s own timeline, such applications are expected to be processed “within weeks.”

[9] The Court has, in many cases, considered the IRCC service standards or processing timelines to determine whether there has been an unreasonable delay. See for instance: Kia v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2026 FC 780 [Kia].

[10] As the Court explained in Kia at para 15: “While not determinative, service standards for study permit applications are relevant to the inquiry of how much time is required by the nature of the process”.

[11] However, the problem in this case is that the Applicant has not adduced any evidence about the IRCC service standards for study permit applications. As IRCC processing timelines vary over time, I cannot determine, in an evidentiary vacuum, which service standard applies in the Applicant’s case. For instance, I note that in Kia, the service standard was 60 days at the time the applicant submitted their study permit application and that “increased to 41 weeks as of February 2025 under the dynamic processing time”, Kia at para 15.

[12] As the Applicant bears the onus of demonstrating that he meets the test for mandamus, I find that the Applicant’s failure to adduce relevant evidence about the service standard undermines his argument about the unreasonableness of the delay.
[13] But even assuming that there has been an unreasonable delay, I find that the Respondent has provided a reasonable justification for the delay.

[14] According to the Global Case Management System notes, on April 30, 2025, the IRCC requested the Applicant to submit his military records. The Applicant responded to the IRCC’s inquiry on May 14, 2025. The Respondent has also provided evidence that no decision has been made due to the pending security screening. The Respondent relies on IRCC’s website to argue that complex or non-routine applications may take “longer than the normal processing time to review” and that given the Applicant’s SP application is undergoing background checks, it can result in longer processing times.

[15] While he was given the opportunity to do so, the Applicant did not make any submission in reply. As such, the Applicant’s only submission before the Court is that the Respondent failed to provide any explanation for the delay.

[16] I acknowledge that the Court has not adopted a uniform approach to deciding whether the need for security checks constitutes a reasonable justification for delay in mandamus cases. I observe that in many cases the Court finds that there is no justification for the delay when the Respondent merely asserts—without filing any evidence—that the application is undergoing security checks or that the Respondent is relying on dated information to justify the delay.

[17] In this case, there is evidence before me indicating that the IRCC was looking into the Applicant’s military record as of May 2025. It offers a reasonable explanation for at least part of the time the IRCC has taken to process the Applicant’s SP application.

[18] For the same reasons, I also find that the Applicant has failed to show that the Respondent has refused to perform their duty. The Respondent was processing the Applicant’s SP application and requesting updated information; it has referred the Applicant’s matter for a background check.

[19] Finally, the Applicant submits that the balance of convenience favours him as he has “endured an excessive wait for a final decision” and the Respondent has failed to provide any justification for the delay. I have rejected both arguments, thus leading me to conclude that the balance of convenience does not favour the issuance of a mandamus order.
III. Conclusion [20] The application for judicial review is dismissed. There will be no costs.

JUDGMENT in IMM-7376-25
THIS COURT’S JUDGMENT is that:
The application for judicial review and request for an order of mandamus is dismissed.
There will be no costs.
